stegosaurus:research:1.title: 2026 in archosaur paleontology (research: General non-avian dinosaur research)

facts.statement: Stegosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, specifically from the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian to Tithonian),

facts.statement: The genus Stegosaurus was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877.
facts.quote: authority: Marsh, 1877

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Stegosaurus is Stegosaurus stenops.
facts.quote: type_species: Stegosaurus stenops

facts.statement: Two other species within the genus are Stegosaurus ungulatus, described in 1879, and Stegosaurus sulcatus, described in 1887.
facts.quote: subdivision: * S. ungulatus Marsh, 1879 S. sulcatus Marsh, 1887

facts.statement: Hypsirhophus and Diracodon have been proposed as synonyms for Stegosaurus.
facts.quote: synonyms: * Hypsirhophus? Cope, 1878 Diracodon Marsh, 1881

facts.statement: Stegosaurus fossils have been found in the western United States and Portugal, dating between 155 and 145 million years ago.
facts.quote: Fossils of the genus have been found in the western United States and in Portugal, where they are found in Kimmeridgian- to Tithonian-aged strata, dating to between 155 and 145 million years ago.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus is characterized by kite-shaped upright plates along its back and spikes on its tail.
facts.quote: characterized by the distinctive kite-shaped upright plates along their backs and spikes on their tails.

facts.statement: It is generally agreed that Stegosaurus used its spiked tails for defense and its plates primarily for display, with secondary thermoregulatory functions.
facts.quote: Today, it is generally agreed that their spiked tails were most likely used for defense against predators, while their plates may have been used primarily for display, and secondarily for thermoregulatory functions.

facts.statement: Due to its short neck and small head, Stegosaurus likely fed on low-lying bushes and shrubs.
facts.quote: It had a short neck and a small head, meaning it most likely ate low-lying bushes and shrubs.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus ungulatus is one of the largest stegosaurians, with specimens reaching about 9 meters in length and weighing over 6.9 metric tons.
facts.quote: One species, Stegosaurus ungulatus, is one of the largest known of all the stegosaurians, with the largest known specimens measuring about 9 m long and weighing over 6.9 MT.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus remains were first identified by Othniel Charles Marsh during the Bone Wars at Dinosaur Ridge National Landmark.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus remains were first identified during the "Bone Wars" by Othniel Charles Marsh at Dinosaur Ridge National Landmark.

facts.statement: Remains of over 80 individual Stegosaurus animals have been discovered.
facts.quote: The remains of over 80 individual animals of this genus have been found.

facts.statement: The first Stegosaurus remains were discovered by Arthur Lakes and H.C. Beckwith in Quarry 5 north of Morrison, Colorado, consisting of caudal vertebrae, a dermal plate, and other postcranial elements.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus, one of the many dinosaurs described in the Bone Wars, was first discovered by Arthur Lakes and H.C. Beckwith, consisting of several caudal vertebrae, a dermal plate, and several additional postcranial elements that were collected north of Morrison, Colorado, at Lakes' YPM Quarry 5.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope named Hypsirhophus discurus in 1878 based on fragmentary fossils from Quarry 3 in Garden Park, Colorado.
facts.quote: On the other side of the Bone Wars, Edward Drinker Cope named Hypsirhophus discurus as another stegosaurian based on fragmentary fossils from Cope's Quarry 3 near the "Cope's Nipple" site in Garden Park, Colorado, in 1878.

facts.statement: Arthur Lakes discovered several large Stegosaurus fossils at Como Bluff, Wyoming, in August 1879.
facts.quote: Arthur Lakes made another discovery later in 1879 at Como Bluff in Albany County, Wyoming, the site also dating to the Upper Jurassic of the Morrison Formation, when he found several large Stegosaurus fossils in August of that year.

facts.statement: The greatest Stegosaurus discovery was a nearly complete, articulated subadult skeleton found in 1885, which included a complete skull and articulated plates.
facts.quote: The greatest Stegosaurus discovery came in 1885 with the discovery of a nearly complete, articulated skeleton of a subadult that included previously undiscovered elements like a complete skull, throat ossicles, and articulated plates.

facts.statement: Marshall P. Felch collected the nearly complete Stegosaurus skeleton between 1885 and 1886 from his quarry in Garden Park, Colorado.
facts.quote: Marshall P. Felch collected the skeleton throughout 1885 and 1886 from Morrison Formation strata at his quarry in Garden Park, a town near Cañon City, Colorado.

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh named the nearly complete skeleton Stegosaurus stenops in 1887.
facts.quote: The skeleton was shipped to Marsh in 1887, who named it Stegosaurus stenops ( "narrow-faced roof lizard") that year.

facts.statement: Marsh initially hypothesized that Stegosaurus was an aquatic, turtle-like animal and believed its plates lay flat over its back like roof shingles.
facts.quote: Marsh initially believed the remains were from an aquatic turtle-like animal, and the basis for its scientific name, 'roof(ed) lizard' was due to his early belief that the plates lay flat over the animal's back, overlapping like the shingles (tiles) on a roof.

facts.statement: Analysis has revealed that the holotype specimen of Stegosaurus armatus is dubious, leading to the replacement of the type species.
facts.quote: Though several more complete specimens have been attributed to Stegosaurus armatus, preparation of the bones and analysis has discovered that this type specimen is actually dubious, which is not an ideal situation for the type species of a well-known genus like Stegosaurus.

facts.statement: While many researchers consider Hypsirhophus a synonym of Stegosaurus, Peter Galton (2010) suggested it is distinct based on vertebral differences.
facts.quote: Many later researchers have considered Hypsirhophus to be a synonym of Stegosaurus, though Peter Galton (2010) suggested that it is distinct based on differences in the vertebrae.

facts.statement: A large spike preserved in Stegosaurus sulcatus has been speculated to be a shoulder spike used for species diagnosis.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus sulcatus most notably preserves a large spike that has been speculated to have been a shoulder spike that is used to diagnose the species.

facts.statement: The type skeleton of Stegosaurus stenops has been on display at the National Museum of Natural History in Washington D.C. since 1915.
facts.quote: The skeleton of S. stenops has since been deposited at the National Museum of Natural History in Washington D. C., where it has been on display since 1915.

facts.statement: A composite Stegosaurus mount at the National Museum of Natural History was created using specimens collected at Quarry 13, Como Bluff, in 1887.
facts.quote: Another mount was made for the NMNH in the form of a mounted composite skeleton consisting of several specimens referred to S. stenops that were collected at Quarry 13 at Como Bluff in 1887, the most complete being USNM 6531.

facts.statement: Richard Swann Lull incorporated the type specimen of Stegosaurus ungulatus into the world's first mounted Stegosaurus skeleton at the Peabody Museum of Natural History in 1910.
facts.quote: The type specimen of S. ungulatus (YPM 1853) was incorporated into the first ever mounted skeleton of a stegosaur at the Peabody Museum of Natural History in 1910 by Richard Swann Lull.

facts.statement: Frederick Lucas named the species Stegosaurus marshi in 1901.
facts.quote: The next species of Stegosaurus to be named was S. marshi by Frederick Lucas in 1901.

facts.statement: Until 1918, the only mounted Stegosaurus skeleton in existence was O.C. Marsh's type specimen of S. ungulatus, displayed at the Peabody Museum of Natural History since 1910.
facts.quote: Until 1918, the only mounted skeleton of Stegosaurus in the world was O. C. Marsh's type specimen of S. ungulatus at the Peabody Museum of Natural History, which was put on display in 1910.

facts.statement: Charles Gilmore directed the creation of the second mounted Stegosaurus skeleton, the first to depict S. stenops, which was completed in 1918 at the U.S. National Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: 1918 saw the completion of the second Stegosaurus mount, and the first depicting S. stenops. This mount was created under the direction of Charles Gilmore at the U.S. National Museum of Natural History.

facts.statement: A composite mounted skeleton of Stegosaurus stenops was displayed at the American Museum of Natural History in 1932.
facts.quote: A third mounted skeleton of Stegosaurus, referred to S. stenops, was put on display at the American Museum of Natural History in 1932.

facts.statement: A composite mount of Stegosaurus ungulatus made from fossils collected at Dinosaur National Monument between 1920 and 1922 was displayed at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in 1940.
facts.quote: Another composite mount, using specimens referred to S. ungulatus collected from Dinosaur National Monument between 1920 and 1922, was put on display at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in 1940.

facts.statement: The American Museum of Natural History launched an expedition in 1897 that found incomplete Stegosaurus specimens at Bone Cabin Quarry, Como Bluff.
facts.quote: The American Museum of Natural History was the first to launch an expedition in 1897, finding several assorted, but incomplete, Stegosaurus specimens at Bone Cabin Quarry in Como Bluff.

facts.statement: Carnegie crews discovered dozens of Stegosaurus specimens at Dinosaur National Monument between the 1900s and 1920s.
facts.quote: in the 1900s-1920s Carnegie crews at Dinosaur National Monument discovered dozens of Stegosaurus specimens in one of the greatest single sites for the taxon.

facts.statement: Carnegie crews found a Stegosaurus cranium (CM 12000), which is one of the few known.
facts.quote: A cranium (CM 12000) was also found by Carnegie crews, one of the few known.

facts.statement: Four different arrangements for the back plates of Stegosaurus have been proposed throughout history.
facts.quote: Four possible plate arrangements have been proposed over the years

facts.statement: O.C. Marsh initially interpreted Stegosaurus plates as lying flat like shingles, an idea that led to the nickname 'roof lizard'.
facts.quote: The plates lie flat along the back, as a shingle-like armor. This was Marsh's initial interpretation, which led to the name 'roof lizard'.

facts.statement: In 1891, O.C. Marsh proposed an arrangement of Stegosaurus plates in a single row along the back.
facts.quote: By 1891, Marsh published a more familiar view of Stegosaurus, with a single row of plates.

facts.statement: Charles R. Knight's 1901 reconstruction and the 1933 film King Kong depicted Stegosaurus plates arranged in two parallel rows along the back.
facts.quote: The plates were paired in a double row along the back, such as in Knight's 1901 reconstruction and the 1933 film King Kong.

facts.statement: By the early 1960s, the arrangement of Stegosaurus plates in two staggered rows became the prevailing theory, supported by partially articulated fossils of S. stenops.
facts.quote: Two rows of alternating plates. By the early 1960s, this had become (and remains) the prevalent idea, mainly because some S. stenops fossils in which the plates are still partially articulated show this arrangement.

facts.statement: The staggered row arrangement of Stegosaurus plates is chiral, meaning left and right sides are distinct mirror images.
facts.quote: This arrangement is chiral and so demands that a specimen be distinguished from its distinct, hypothetical mirror-image form.

facts.statement: Frederick Lucas commissioned artist Charles R. Knight to create a life restoration of Stegosaurus ungulatus based on his interpretation of paired plates.
facts.quote: Lucas commissioned Charles R. Knight to produce a life restoration of S. ungulatus based on his new interpretation.

facts.statement: Richard Swann Lull suggested in 1910 that the alternating plate pattern in S. stenops fossils resulted from the skeleton shifting after death.
facts.quote: In 1910, Richard Swann Lull wrote that the alternating pattern seen in S. stenops was probably due to shifting of the skeleton after death.

facts.statement: Charles Gilmore argued in 1914 that Stegosaurus plates were preserved in alternating rows in the fossil record without evidence of post-mortem shifting.
facts.quote: In 1914, Charles Gilmore argued against Lull's interpretation, noting that several specimens of S. stenops, including the now-completely prepared holotype, preserved the plates in alternating rows near the peak of the back, and that there was no evidence of the plates having shifted relative to the body during fossilization.

facts.statement: The interpretation of alternating plates proposed by Gilmore and Lucas became the standard, leading to a remount of the Peabody Museum skeleton in 1924.
facts.quote: Gilmore and Lucas' interpretation became the generally accepted standard, and Lull's mount at the Peabody Museum was changed to reflect this in 1924.

facts.statement: Fossils collected by the American Museum of Natural History and the Carnegie Museum of Natural History have been assigned to the species Stegosaurus ungulatus.
facts.quote: Both the AMNH and CM material has been referred to Stegosaurus ungulatus.

facts.statement: A significant Stegosaurus fossil was discovered in 1937 at Garden Park by high school teacher Frank Kessler.
facts.quote: An important discovery came in 1937 again at Garden Park by a high school teacher named Frank Kessler

facts.statement: Paleontologist Robert Landberg excavated a 70% complete Stegosaurus skeleton at the site nicknamed 'The Kessler Site'.
facts.quote: Landberg excavated the skeleton with the DMNS crews, recovering a 70% complete Stegosaurus skeleton

facts.statement: The Stegosaurus skeleton from the Kessler Site was mounted at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science in 1938.
facts.quote: Phillip Reinheimer, a steel worker, mounted the Stegosaurus skeleton at the DMNS in 1938

facts.statement: A nearly complete Stegosaurus skeleton was found near the Kessler Site by Bryan Small, after whom the site was named.
facts.quote: The expedition was successful in finding a nearly complete Stegosaurus near the Kessler site by Bryan Small

facts.statement: Harold Bollan discovered a 40% complete Stegosaurus skeleton in Rabbit Valley, Mesa County, Colorado, in 1987.
facts.quote: In 1987, a 40% complete Stegosaurus skeleton was discovered in Rabbit Valley in Mesa County, Colorado, by Harold Bollan

facts.statement: The specimen known as 'Sophie' is 85% intact and contains 360 bones, making it the best-preserved Stegosaurus.
facts.quote: Sophie the Stegosaurus is the best preserved Stegosaurus specimen, being 85% intact and containing 360 bones

facts.statement: The 'Sophie' Stegosaurus was discovered in 2003 by Bob Simon at a quarry near Shell, Wyoming.
facts.quote: Sophie was first discovered by Bob Simon in 2003 at a quarry on the Red Canyon Ranch near Shell, Wyoming

facts.statement: Stegosaurus is a quadrupedal dinosaur identified by a double row of vertical kite-shaped plates on its back and two pairs of horizontal spikes at the tail's end.
facts.quote: The quadrupedal Stegosaurus is one of the most easily identifiable dinosaur genera, due to the distinctive double row of kite-shaped plates rising vertically along the rounded back and the two pairs of long spikes extending horizontally near the end of the tail

facts.statement: S. stenops measured 6.5 meters long with a mass of 3.5 metric tons, while S. ungulatus measured 7 meters long with a mass of 3.8 metric tons.
facts.quote: S. stenops reached 6.5 m in length and 3.5 MT in body mass, while S. ungulatus reached 7 m in length and 3.8 MT in body mass

facts.statement: Some large Stegosaurus individuals may have reached lengths of 7.5 to 9 meters and masses of 5.0 to 5.3 metric tons.
facts.quote: Some large individuals may have reached 7.5-9 m in length and 5.0 - 5.3 MT in body mass

facts.statement: A subadult Stegosaurus specimen discovered in Wyoming in 1994 was 4.6 meters long, 2 meters high, and weighed between 1.5 and 2.2 metric tons.
facts.quote: One subadult specimen, discovered in 1994 in Wyoming, is 4.6 m long and 2 m high, and is estimated to have weighed 1.5-2.2 metric tons (1.6-2.4 short tons) while alive

facts.statement: A Stegosaurus specimen from Portugal was originally thought to belong to the Alcobaça Formation but was later suggested to be from the Lourinhã Formation.
facts.quote: In 2007, Escaso and colleagues described a Stegosaurus specimen from the Casal Novo locality of Portugal, originally thought to be part of the Alcobaça Formation, and subsequently suggested to be part of the Lourinhã Formation

facts.statement: Stegosaurus had a long, narrow skull that was small relative to its body size.
facts.quote: The long and narrow skull was small in proportion to the body.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the low position of the skull indicates Stegosaurus likely browsed low-growing vegetation.
facts.quote: The skull's low position suggests that Stegosaurus may have been a browser of low-growing vegetation.

facts.statement: Stegosaurian teeth were small, triangular, and flat, with wear patterns indicating they ground their food.
facts.quote: Stegosaurian teeth were small, triangular, and flat; wear facets show that they did grind their food.

facts.statement: Despite its large body size, the braincase of Stegosaurus was small, comparable in size to that of a dog.
facts.quote: Despite the animal's overall size, the braincase of Stegosaurus was small, being no larger than that of a dog.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus stenops has 27 vertebrae before the sacrum, a sacrum with four vertebrae in most subadults, and approximately 46 tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: In Stegosaurus stenops there are 27 bones in the vertebral column anterior to the sacrum, a varying number of vertebrae in the sacrum, with four in most subadults, and around 46 caudal (tail) vertebrae.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus had three short toes on each hind foot and five toes on each fore foot, with only the inner two fore toes having a blunt hoof.
facts.quote: The hind feet each had three short toes, while each fore foot had five toes; only the inner two toes had a blunt hoof.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus had much shorter forelimbs than its stocky hindlimbs, resulting in an unusual posture.
facts.quote: The fore limbs were much shorter than the stocky hind limbs, which resulted in an unusual posture.

facts.statement: The tail of Stegosaurus was likely held off the ground, while its head was positioned low, probably no higher than 1 meter above the ground.
facts.quote: The tail appears to have been held well clear of the ground, while the head of Stegosaurus was positioned relatively low down, probably no higher than 1 m above the ground.

facts.statement: The dermal plates of Stegosaurus were not directly attached to the skeleton but arose from the skin.
facts.quote: They were not directly attached to the animal's skeleton, instead arising from the skin.

facts.statement: Well-preserved impressions of Hesperosaurus plates show a smooth surface with grooves, indicating the plates were covered in keratinous sheaths.
facts.quote: Well preserved integumentary impressions of the plates of Hesperosaurus show a smooth surface with long and parallel, shallow grooves. This indicates that the plates were covered in keratinous sheaths.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus fossils date to the Late Jurassic period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Jurásico Superior

facts.statement: The genus Stegosaurus was named by Marsh in 1877.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Marsh, 1877

facts.statement: The type species Stegosaurus stenops was named by Marsh in 1887.
facts.quote: type_species_authority: Marsh, 1887

facts.statement: Other species assigned to the genus include Stegosaurus armatus (dubious), Stegosaurus ungulatus, and Stegosaurus sulcatus.
facts.quote: subdivision: Stegosaurus armatus Marsh, 1877 (dudosa) Stegosaurus ungulatus Marsh, 1879 Stegosaurus sulcatus Marsh, 1887

facts.statement: Stegosauridae members are found across the Northern Hemisphere, Africa, and possibly South America.
facts.quote: This group is widespread, with members across the Northern Hemisphere, Africa and possibly South America.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the jaw ridges of Stegosaurus supported a beak or fleshy cheeks, with some researchers suggesting the latter.
facts.quote: Other researchers have interpreted these ridges as modified versions of similar structures in other ornithischians which might have supported fleshy cheeks, rather than beaks.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus is a genus of three, possibly four, known species of thyreophoran stegosaurian dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus (gr. "lagarto con tejado" o "lagarto cubierto"), castellanizado como estegosaurio, es un género con tres, probablemente cuatro, especies conocidas de dinosaurios tireóforos estegosáuridos

facts.statement: Stegosaurus is one of the most recognizable dinosaurs due to its distinctive tail spikes and plates.
facts.quote: Debido a sus distintivas espinas de la cola y placas, Stegosaurus es uno de los más reconocidos dinosaurios

facts.statement: At least three Stegosaurus species have been identified in the upper Morrison Formation of western United States.
facts.quote: Al menos tres especies han sido identificadas en la porción superior de la Formación Morrison, del oeste de Estados Unidos

facts.statement: Remains of at least eighty individuals of Stegosaurus have been found.
facts.quote: Se han encontrado restos de por lo menos ochenta individuos

facts.statement: A Stegosaurus specimen was discovered in Portugal in 2006.
facts.quote: En 2006, se descubrió un espécimen de Stegosaurus en Portugal

facts.statement: Stegosaurus likely lived alongside dinosaurs such as Apatosaurus, Diplodocus, Brachiosaurus, Ceratosaurus, Allosaurus, and Torvosaurus, with the latter being possible predators.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus habría vivido junto a dinosaurios como Apatosaurus, Diplodocus, Brachiosaurus, Ceratosaurus, Allosaurus y Torvosaurus, siendo estos últimos sus posibles predadores

facts.statement: Stegosaurus was a large, heavily built quadrupedal herbivore with a distinctive posture featuring a strongly arched back, short front limbs, a head near the ground, and a stiff tail held in the air.
facts.quote: Siendo un gran herbívoro cuadrúpedo, pesadamente constituido, Stegosaurus tenía una distintiva e inusual postura, con un lomo fuertemente arqueado, los miembros anteriores cortos, la cabeza cerca del suelo y la cola rígida sostenida en el aire

facts.statement: Stegosaurus's arsenal of plates and spikes has been the subject of many hypotheses.
facts.quote: Su arsenal de placas y de púas ha sido el tema de muchas conjeturas

facts.statement: The tail spikes were likely used for defense, while the plates have been proposed as defensive mechanisms, display structures, and thermoregulation tools.
facts.quote: Las espinas fueron utilizadas muy probablemente para la defensa, mientras que las placas también se han propuesto como mecanismo defensivo, y como parte de la exhibición y de las funciones de regulación térmica

facts.statement: Stegosaurus had a relatively low brain-to-body mass ratio.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus tenía una proporción de masa cerebral a cuerpo relativamente baja

facts.statement: Stegosaurus had a short neck and small head, suggesting it likely fed on low bushes and plants.
facts.quote: Tenía un cuello corto y una cabeza pequeña, lo que significa que probablemente comía arbustos y plantas bajos

facts.statement: The species Stegosaurus ungulatus was one of the largest stegosaurians, larger than Kentrosaurus and Huayangosaurus, and approximately the size of a bus.
facts.quote: Una de sus especies, Stegosaurus ungulatus, fue uno de los más grandes estegosaurianos, más grande que Kentrosaurus y que Huayangosaurus y aunque aproximadamente del tamaño de un autobús

facts.statement: Large individuals of Stegosaurus could grow up to 9 meters long, 4 meters high, and weigh between 5.3 and 7 metric tons.
facts.quote: Aunque los individuos grandes, YPM Coll, podían crecer hasta 9 metros de largo y de 4 metros de alto y entre 5,3 y 7 toneladas de masa corporal

facts.statement: In 2016, Gregory S. Paul estimated S. stenops to be 6.5 meters long and 3.5 metric tons, and S. ungulatus to be 7 meters long and 3.8 metric tons.
facts.quote: En 2016, Gregory S. Paul presentó una estimación más baja de 6,5 metros de longitud y 3,5 toneladas métricas de masa corporal para S. stenops, y 7 metros de longitud y 3,8 toneladas de masa corporal para S. ungulatus

facts.statement: Most known information about Stegosaurus comes from mature animal remains, though juvenile specimens have recently been found.
facts.quote: La mayor parte de la información conocida sobre Stegosaurus viene de restos de animales maduros, si bien se han encontrado recientemente restos de ejemplares juveniles

facts.statement: A subadult specimen discovered in Wyoming in 1994 measured 4.6 meters long, 2 meters high, and is estimated to have weighed 2.3 metric tons in life.
facts.quote: Un espécimen subadulto descubierto en 1994 en Wyoming mide 4,6 metros de largo y 2 metros de alto, y se considera que pesaría en vida 2,3 toneladas

facts.statement: The smallest known Stegosaurus skeleton measures 210 centimeters long and 80 centimeters high to the back.
facts.quote: El esqueleto más pequeño conocido mide 210 centímetros de largo y 80 centímetros de alto hasta el lomo

facts.statement: Stegosaurus had three short toes on its hind feet and five toes on each front foot, with only the two inner front toes being hoof-like.
facts.quote: Las patas traseras tenían tres dedos cortos, mientras que cada pata delantera tenía cinco dedos; solamente los dos dedos internos tenían forma de casco

facts.statement: The phalangeal formula of Stegosaurus is 2-2-2-2-1.
facts.quote: La fórmula falángica es 2-2-2-2-1

facts.statement: Stegosaurus likely held its tail well away from the ground while its head was positioned near the ground, probably no more than 1 meter off the ground.
facts.quote: La cola parece haber sido sostenida bien lejos de la tierra, mientras que la cabeza de tenía una posición cerca al suelo, probablemente a no más de 1 metro del suelo

facts.statement: Stegosaurus had a long, narrow skull that was small in proportion to its body.
facts.quote: El largo y angosto cráneo era pequeño en proporción con el cuerpo

facts.statement: The low position of the skull suggests Stegosaurus may have been a browser of low-growing vegetation.
facts.quote: El cráneo en la posición baja sugiere que Stegosaurus puede haber sido un ramoneador de la vegetación de crecimiento bajo

facts.statement: Stegosaurus lacked front teeth, which were replaced by a horny beak or rhamphotheca.
facts.quote: La ausencia de dientes delanteros y su reemplazo por un pico córneo o rhamphotheca

facts.statement: The lower jaw had flat extensions downward and upward that would have completely hidden the teeth when viewed from the side.
facts.quote: La mandíbula inferior tenía extensiones planas hacia abajo y hacia arriba que habrían ocultado por completo los dientes vistos desde un lado

facts.statement: These jaw structures likely supported a turtle-like beak in life.
facts.quote: Estos probablemente sostenían un pico de tortuga en vida

facts.statement: Stegosaurus had small, triangular teeth with flat facets from wear, indicating it ground its food.
facts.quote: Los dientes de Stegosaurus eran pequeños y triangulares; las facetas planas por el desgaste indican que molían su alimento

facts.statement: The jaw insertion position suggests Stegosaurus had cheeks to keep food in the mouth while chewing.
facts.quote: La posición de inserción de las quijadas sugiere que Stegosaurus tenía mejillas para mantener el alimento en la boca mientras masticaba

facts.statement: A well-preserved braincase mold showed that Stegosaurus had a very small brain, possibly the smallest among dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Ese molde demostró que el cerebro era, de hecho, muy pequeño: quizá el más pequeño entre los dinosaurios

facts.statement: The fact that a Stegosaurus weighing over 4.5 tons could have a brain of no more than 80 grams contributed to the popular idea that dinosaurs were stupid.
facts.quote: El hecho de que un animal que pesaba más de 4,5 toneladas pudiera tener un cerebro de no más de 80 gramos contribuyó a sostener la vieja idea popular de que los dinosaurios eran estúpidos

facts.statement: Stegosaurus remains were first identified by Othniel Charles Marsh during the "Bone Wars" at Dinosaur Ridge National Monument.
facts.quote: Los restos de Stegosaurus fueron identificados por primera vez durante las "Guerras de los Huesos" por Othniel Charles Marsh en el Monumento Nacional Dinosaur Ridge

facts.statement: The first known Stegosaurus skeletons were fragmentary with scattered bones, and it took many years to understand their true appearance.
facts.quote: Los primeros esqueletos conocidos eran fragmentarios y los huesos estaban dispersos, y pasarían muchos años antes de que se entendiera bien la verdadera apariencia de estos animales

facts.statement: Stegosaurus belongs to the parent group Stegosaurinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Stegosaurinae

facts.statement: Stegosaurus belongs to the family Stegosauridae.
facts.quote: Family: Stegosauridae

facts.statement: Stegosaurus is classified in the class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: Stegosaurus lived during the late Jurassic Period, approximately between 156 and 144 million years ago, from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages.
facts.quote: que vivieron a finales del período Jurásico, hace aproximadamente entre 156 y 144 millones de años, entre el Kimmeridgiense y el Titoniense

facts.statement: Stegosaurus lived in what is now North America and possibly Europe.
facts.quote: en lo que hoy es América del Norte y posiblemente Europa

facts.statement: The genus Stegosaurus has a recorded time range from the Oxfordian to the Cenomanian (161.5 to 93.9 million years ago).
facts.quote: Time range: Oxfordian to Cenomanian (161.5 to 93.9 million years ago)

facts.statement: There are 86 recorded fossil occurrences of Stegosaurus in the Paleobiology Database.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 86

facts.statement: The fourth species, Stegosaurus armatus, is considered doubtful.
facts.quote: con una cuarta Stegosaurus armatus siendo dudosa

facts.statement: Some researchers interpret the beak-like structures as modified versions of similar structures in other ornithischians that could have supported fleshy cheeks instead of beaks.
facts.quote: Otros investigadores han interpretado estas crestas como versiones modificadas de estructuras similares en otros ornitisquios que podrían haber soportado mejillas carnosas, en lugar de picos

facts.statement: The presence of an extended beak along most of the jaws may have prevented the presence of cheeks in these species.
facts.quote: La presencia de un pico extendido a lo largo de gran parte de las mandíbulas puede haber impedido la presencia de mejillas en estas especies

facts.statement: The effective anatomy of the Stegosaurus brain is poorly known.
facts.quote: La anatomía efectiva del cerebro de Stegosaurus es poco conocida
